DIRECTOR'S INSPECTION RIGHTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — DIRECTOR'S INSPECTION RIGHTS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., a California corporation, and to Jordan Lee's status as a director of Acme, Inc. It describes the statutory right a California corporation's director has to inspect and copy the corporation's books, records, and documents, and to inspect its physical properties -- a right that belongs to a director personally, arising from the director's own oversight role on the board, and that is distinct from the shareholder's inspection right described in this project's separate Shareholder and Member Inspection Rights information sheet.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a demand on Acme, Inc., and it does not resolve any dispute about whether Jordan Lee is a currently serving director of Acme, Inc. at the time inspection is sought. This document is not this project's Corporate Bylaws document, which governs Acme, Inc.'s internal affairs generally; this document instead focuses specifically on the director-inspection statute.

DIRECTOR'S ABSOLUTE RIGHT TO INSPECT BOOKS, RECORDS, DOCUMENTS, AND PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
California's General Corporation Law gives every director an "absolute right" -- that is the statute's own wording, not a court's characterization of it -- at any reasonable time, to inspect and copy all books, records, and documents of every kind, and to inspect the physical properties, of the corporation of which the person is a director, and also of its subsidiary corporations, whether domestic or foreign. On its face, this right is broader in category than a shareholder's separate books-and-records right described elsewhere in this document (which reaches accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings): the director's right reaches all books, records, and documents of every kind, plus the corporation's physical properties, without that narrower accounting-and-minutes framing. The statute's text does not condition this right on the director stating any purpose at all, unlike the shareholder's right, which the statute expressly limits to a "purpose reasonably related to" the shareholder's interest -- § 1602 contains no comparable qualifying language. Inspection by a director may be made in person or through an agent or attorney, and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts; the statute does not state any express limit on that agent-or-attorney method. Finally, the statute expressly extends to a director of a foreign corporation that has its principal office in California or that customarily holds its board meetings in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every director shall have the absolute right at any reasonable time to inspect and copy all books, records and documents of every kind and to inspect the physical properties of the corporation of which such person is a director and also of its subsidiary corporations, domestic or foreign. Such inspection by a director may be made in person or by agent or attorney and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts. This section applies to a director of any foreign corporation having its principal office in California or customarily holding meetings of its board in California."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1602 (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, director's right to inspect books, records, documents, and physical properties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1602.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, distinctly-worded director right -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation or about how a court would resolve a dispute over what is "reasonable" timing for a particular inspection. Unlike the shareholder inspection statutes described elsewhere in this document (Corp. Code §§ 1600(d), 1601(b)), which each expressly state that the right "may not be limited by the articles or bylaws," § 1602 contains no equivalent non-waivability sentence of its own; this document does not claim, and did not find support for, a rule that a corporation's articles or bylaws cannot limit a director's own inspection right -- that question is left open rather than assumed either way. This document also does not resolve what counts as a "reasonable time" for a given inspection, or what happens to this right once a person's board service ends, both of which the statute leaves undefined. Section 1602 is a single, undivided statutory paragraph with no lettered subsections, so only one citation is offered below; there is no second subsection of this section to disclose as non-independent of it.

COURT REMEDY FOR A REFUSED INSPECTION DEMAND, READ AGAINST A REFUSED DIRECTOR DEMAND
California's inspection chapter gives a court a remedy phrased generally around "a lawful demand for inspection," not phrased around a shareholder's demand specifically: upon refusal of a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county may enforce the right of inspection on just and proper conditions, or, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the corporation's books and records and investigate its property, funds, and affairs (including those of its subsidiaries), and report to the court. This remedy provision is codified in the same chapter of the Corporations Code -- captioned "Rights of Inspection" and spanning sections 1600 through 1605 -- as the director's own inspection right, and its own wording does not single out shareholder demands, so its enforcement mechanism reads as available for a refused director demand as well as a refused shareholder demand.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon refusal of a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county, may enforce the right of inspection with just and proper conditions or may, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the books and records kept in this state and investigate the property, funds and affairs of any domestic corporation or any foreign corporation keeping records in this state and of any subsidiary corporation thereof, domestic or foreign, keeping records in this state and to report thereon in such manner as the court may direct."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, court enforcement of a refused inspection demand (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1603.)
  "CHAPTER 16. Rights of Inspection [1600 - 1605]"
  — Cal. Corp. Code, Division 1, Chapter 16 caption (California Legislative Information text, displayed on the section 1602 page), California General Corporation Law, chapter caption identifying sections 1600 through 1605 as a single chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1602.)
  Known gap: Section 1602 does not itself state a remedy or cross-reference the remedy section by number, and the remedy section does not name directors or cite section 1602 specifically -- its "lawful demand for inspection" language is chapter-general wording rather than an explicit statutory cross-reference naming the director's right. This clause's application of that remedy to a refused director demand is therefore a structural reading, based on the statute's placement within the same inspection chapter and the remedy provision's own unqualified wording, not an express statutory statement that the remedy section covers a section 1602 refusal; no court decision confirming this reading was located and verified for this document, so this document does not claim one exists. This corpus's existing Shareholder and Member Inspection Rights information sheet already documents this same remedy section's fuller mechanics as applied to a refused shareholder demand -- the officers'-and-agents' duty to produce records to a court-appointed inspector on penalty of contempt, and the default rule that the person who sought the audit bears its expense unless the court shifts that cost to the corporation -- and this document does not restate those additional subsections separately. The chapter-heading citation below is pulled from the same California Legislative Information display page as section 1602 itself, offered only as evidence of the Corporations Code's own chapter organization, not as an independent source from the statutory text it appears alongside.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — DIRECTOR'S INSPECTION RIGHTS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme, Inc. was prepared by Jordan Lee.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
Position held at Acme, Inc.: Director

[This information sheet describes the California statute giving a corporation's director the right to inspect and copy the corporation's books, records, and documents, and to inspect its physical properties (Cal. Corp. Code § 1602), and the related court remedy for a refused demand. It is not a completed demand, does not itself compel Acme, Inc. to permit any inspection, and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]
